2 months ago, our team took 2nd place in the Scientific Discovery track at the Codex & AITX Community hackathon, where Rishi Golla , Abheek Pradhan , Armaan Amatya , and I worked on reproducing results from ML papers. Since then, Abheek, Armaan, and I have had the opportunity to keep exploring that problem with the DeepInvent team, pushing further on AutoResearch and systems that can take an initial idea, figure out how to test it, run experiments, and determine whether the results actually hold up. Testing our own system through DeepInvent made a broader challenge in AutoResearch clear - evals. Generating hypotheses is one challenge, but proving them through experiments is much harder, especially when the goal of these systems is to identify unexplored whitespace in research. Grateful to everyone who helped kick this work off, and to Marcus Weller and the rest of the Deepinvent team for giving us the opportunity to keep pushing innovation forward. More soon. ...more

Stranded in Chicago. Late to the hackathon. Still won and walked away with $2,500 and one of the best experiences we’ve had as a team. What started as a stressful, chaotic trip (flights, hotel issues - we were literally on the streets until 4 AM) turned into one of the most valuable experiences I’ve had so far. At the OnionDAO hackathon, I worked with an incredible team - Haotian Li and Sulayman Bowles - and together we built PayrollPro: We combined confidential transfers, multisig wallets, and Solana Pay into a working prototype - a USD-pegged stablecoin with private salary payments, secure multisig treasury management, and instant payouts via QR codes. The goal: privacy, security, and real usability, all built on Token-2022. Features: - 100% confidential transfers - Yield strategies to earn on USDC - Multisig corporate treasuries - Automated payroll management - Token-2022 extensions Tech stack: React, TypeScript, Rust, Firebase, Gill Framework, Surfpool And honestly? The prize wasn’t the most valuable part. It was the teamwork, the late-night problem solving, the people we met at the co-working space, and getting lost in the city along the way. Thank you to the Solana Foundation and Midwest Blockchain Conference for the opportunity. We’re excited to keep building and exploring opportunities in Web3. If you’re working on something in this space, or know of upcoming events, let’s connect. #hackathon #web3 #solana #blockchain #studentdeveloper #buildinpublic #startuplife #react #rust #typescript #token2022 ...more

In April, I moved to Austin. In May, I won the Bioscience Prize at the AITX Community x Antler × OpenAI Codex hackathon, presented by Dr. Marcus Weller . And in August, I started my journey as a Founder in Residence at Antler and joined Gamma ’s Ambassador Council. Austin has truly surprised me. But what looks like four months of progress was actually three years in the making. Three years of rejections, attempts, mistakes, rebuilding, and learning. Grateful for the journey. Still learning. Still building.

Over the past 10 weeks, I had the opportunity to intern at McLane Company as a Software Infrastructure Intern on the Platform Admin team. Throughout the summer, I got hands-on exposure to how a large-scale enterprise keeps its systems running 24/7 - learning how servers are deployed and maintained to support applications and business operations around the clock. I dove into Kubernetes and cluster architecture, and spent significant time working in Dynatrace on server monitoring and cost optimization, identifying ways to bring visibility into infrastructure spend across the organization. Equally valuable was working alongside teams across IT, seeing firsthand how operations run at scale and how infrastructure decisions ripple across the business. I closed out the internship with a presentation to the Executive Leadership Team on my server monitoring and cost optimization work. I'm incredibly grateful to McLane for giving me the opportunity to share my findings directly with leadership. I want to sincerely thank my manager, Anand Pandey , for his mentorship and guidance throughout the summer, and Shivani Agarwal for her leadership and support at the VP level. Thank you also to Idowu Ademoye and Kenneth Hudgins , who I worked with most closely and who helped me push through technical hurdles and build my knowledge of McLane's systems. I also want to thank Casie Clark and Zachery Johnson, MBA for their leadership of the intern program and for giving me the opportunity to thrive this summer. Lastly, thank you to Dave Morehead for mentoring me throughout the internship. This internship taught me an enormous amount, both technically and practically, and I'm walking away with a much deeper appreciation for what it takes to keep enterprise infrastructure running at scale. I'm excited to carry that forward into the next stage of my career in tech.

I spent this past week at GE Vernova's ENERGY2LEAD conference in Greenville, SC. A few days with 26 other students, a business challenge, and more time on the floor of the world's largest heavy-duty gas turbine plant than I expected to get. It's hard to overstate the scale. Roughly a quarter of the world's electricity is generated on GE Vernova technology, and you feel that standing next to a machine that weighs half a million pounds and is still built to tolerances finer than a human hair. Reading that is one thing. Standing next to it is another. What surprised me most was how much of the week was built around us rather than around the company. Communication workshops, a business challenge, and a lot of unstructured time with engineers who were honest about their own paths. I came in expecting to learn about turbines. I left understanding myself better, and with a much clearer picture of what I want the next few years to look like. The other thing that stuck: the Edison Engineering Development Program. The Edison Engineers who came to talk with us were the most enthusiastic people in the building. That said more about how GE Vernova treats development than any slide could, and one of them explained how the program let her pursue a master's alongside industry work, which reframed a decision I'd been going back and forth on for a while. Greenville was a nice surprise too. The site isn't an office park in the middle of nowhere. It's a real city with a walkable downtown, beautiful greenery, and a waterfall in the middle of it. Thank you to Nam Tran for pointing me toward this in the first place, and to Ja'Net Vicks, MBA and the entire GE Vernova team for putting this together. And to the other 26 students who made it a genuinely good few days.

“If I die, it would rather be the mountain.” Those words from Nirmal ‘Nims’ Purja weren’t about chasing danger. They were about living with purpose. And sadly, today those words came true. It was the darkest day for mountaineering community, in fact every Nepali. From completing all 14 peaks above 8,000 meters in record time, to leading daring high-altitude rescues, he inspired millions to dream bigger and push beyond perceived limits. Whether you climb mountains, or climb your dreams, you are constantly fighting through life’s challenges. Rest in peace, Nims. Nepal lost a hero. The world lost one of the greatest climbers of our generation 🏔️ 🇳🇵 😢 #randomtopics

This one hurts. Pretty dark day for Nepal. Rest in peace, Nimsdai. Nirmal Purja came from just a small village in the Dhaulagiri foothills, but eventually gained global recognition for his crazy mountaineering efforts. He starred in the Netflix documentary "14 Peaks", but what he should be most known for is something simpler but way more profound, giving Nepali people hope and optimism. People coming from small countries understand this deeply. We don't have many role models in the big "world stage." We cheer everyone of our own. We're still not that far removed from the agricultural subsistence farming lifestyle of our parents/grandparents, so seeing someone succeed and inspire people on the global stage is very rare. Nimsdai is 1 of 1 in this regard. There are very few people bringing an entire country together, and it is devastating to see his light extinguished. I am inspired everyday to work as hard as I do, to have some sort of similar impact in the world stage. Here's to you, Nimsdai. We all have to climb our own mountains, you've shown us how to do so!

I thought I understood what it meant to build a company. Then I went to Y Combinator Startup School. I saw some of the strongest names in startups like Vinod Khosla, Patrick Collison, Gerry Tan, etc. Sitting in a space with that level of ambition is incredibly humbling. When you build on your own, you convince yourself you are moving fast. Being surrounded by founders at this caliber completely shatters your baseline. Sam Altman talked about how finding your specific niche is actually getting easier. Alexandr Wang explained how open source tools are completely lowering the barrier to entry. Jensen Huang made it clear that coming in with zero experience is often your biggest advantage. The biggest takeaway was not a specific growth strategy. It was realizing the best builders are simply obsessed with shrinking their learning curves. They do not wait for perfect conditions. They just ship and adapt. I walked in hoping to validate my own ideas. I walked out with an entirely new standard for execution. I am incredibly grateful to have been in the Chase Center this weekend, and as a Warriors fan this was a dream come true. Thank you to Y Combinator for putting together an experience I will never forget. #yc #ycstartupschool
